pride_data.title: Structural Insights into Complement Inhibition: Visualizing Distinct Binding Modes of C4b-binding Protein Complexes with C4b and SAP
pride_data.projectDescription: C4b-binding protein (C4BP) is an innate immune inhibitor found in serum. Human C4BP adopts spider-like higher-order structures (HOS) formed by disulfide-linked C4BPα and C4BPβ chains that non-covalently bind vitamin K-dependent protein S (ProS). These spider-like structures can form even larger complexes as C4BP interacts with other, mostly complement-related, proteins. The complement inhibitory role of C4BP is primarily mediated through its interaction with C4b. C4BP also binds with high affinity to serum amyloid P component (SAP), a pentraxin family member associated with amyloidosis conditions. Here, we structurally and compositionally characterize C4BP interactions with these two natively occurring binders. To achieve this, we combine mass photometry, high-speed atomic force microscopy, and cross-linking mass spectrometry. By integrating the results, we reveal two distinct binding modes of C4BP when bound to C4b or SAP. Given the spider-like assembly of C4BP, C4b interacts with the N-terminal region of a single C4BPα leg, enabling multiple C4b molecules to bind to the C4BP HOS. Conversely, SAP engages with the entire spider-like HOS: the C4BPα-C4BPβ oligomerization core binds to the B-face of SAP, and the C4BPα legs wrap around it.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: The experiments were performed using human plasma-purified protein samples (C4BP and C4b) and recombinantly expressed proteins (C4BPα and SAP) were used. The C4BP and C4b samples (Complement Technology, Inc) were purified from healthy, pooled donor plasma of more than 16 donors. Bis(2,5-dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl) glutarate (DSG), 1-(2,5-Dioxocyclopentyl) 8-(2,5-dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl) octanedioate (DSS), and bis(2,5-Dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl) 3,3'-sulfinyldipropionate (DSSO) were acquired from CF Plus Chemicals. The C4BP-C4b were prepared by incubating C4BP or C4BPα 0.1 mg/mL (final concentration) with C4b to achieve 1:1 C4BP:C4b or 2:1 C4BPα:C4b molar ratio (37 °C, 1h, 350 rpm) in 50 mM HEPES, pH = 7.4, 150 mM NaCl. The C4BP-SAP complexes were prepared in a similar manner as the C4BP complexes with C4b. C4BP 0.1 mg/mL (final concentration) was incubated with SAP to achieve 2:1 SAP:C4BP molar ratio (37 °C, 1h, 350 rpm) in 50 mM HEPES, pH = 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2. Cross-linking was performed in an experimental triplicate with DSS, DSG, and DSSO, all at 0.5 mM concentration. The addition of a crosslinker resulted in a final DMSO concentration of 5% (v/v) in the sample. Immediately after the 1 h incubation, the reaction was quenched with 1 M Tris (pH = 8.5) to achieve a final concentration of 50 mM in the sample. The cross-linked samples were denatured by 8 M urea. Reduction and alkylation were performed with 10 mM TCEP and 40 mM CAA (30 min, room temperature (RT)). After, the samples were diluted with N-ethylmpoline buffer (pH = 8.5), to reduce the urea concentration to 2 M. The samples were digested by trypsin (1:20 (w/w)) and LysC (1:50 (w/w)) for 16h, 37 °C. The digestion was stopped by TFA addition (final 0.5% (v/v)), and the resulting peptides were desalted on an Oasis HLB µElution Plate (Waters Corp) using a vendor-provided protocol. Solvent from the desalted peptides was fully evaporated, and the peptides were deglycosylated using a Protein Deglycosylation Mix II (New England Biolabs) according to a vendor-provided protocol. The deglycosylated peptides were desalted, and the solvent was fully evaporated. Prior to the mass spectrometry (MS) analysis, the peptides were dissolved in 2% (v/v) FA.  The liquid chromatography (LC)-MS/MS analysis was performed on an UltiMate 3000 UHPLC system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc). The cross-linked peptides were analyzed in a 90 min gradient. First, the peptides were trapped on an Acclaim Pepmap 100 C18 (5 mm × 0.3 mm, 5 μm, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc) for 1 min at a flow rate of 30 μL/min, solvent A (0.1% FA v/v in H2O). The trapping was followed by a separation on an in-house packed analytical column (Reprosil 2.4 μm, 75 μm × 50 cm) at a flow rate of 0.3 μL/min using a gradient starting from 9% solvent B (80% acetonitrile (ACN) v/v, 0.1% FA v/v) at 0–1 min, 13% B at 2 min; 44% B at 67 min, 55% B 72 min, 99% B 75 min, and equilibrated for the next run in 9% B at 80–90 min. MS1 scans were collected with the following parameters: resolution = 60000, mass range = 375-1600 Th, automatic AGC target and maximum injection time, cycle time = 1s. MS2 scans were collected in data-dependent mode for precursors with charge state above 3, with the following parameters: isolation window = 1.4 Th, resolution = 30000, mass range = 200-2000 Th. Precursors that were once selected for fragmentation were excluded from MS2 for 30 seconds. The peptides were fragmented using stHCD with NCE 19, 25, 31% for DSSO, and NCE 24, 28, 33% for DSG and DSS.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: The resulting raw spectra were searched using pLink 2 against a FASTA file containing common contaminants and the most abundant proteins with IBAQ >9.5 × 106 from the C4BP sample, as identified by bottom-up proteomics. Additionally, the C4A and C4B genes were divided into three separate chains (α, β, and γ), which form the C4b structure. Propeptides and signal peptides were removed from the FASTA file, and SAP sequence was added. In the case of the C4b complex with recombinant C4BPα, the C4BPα sequence was substituted by the recombinant protein sequence. The linker mass cross-linking two lysine residues was set to be 96.021 Da, 138.068 Da, and 158.004 Da for DSG, DSS, and DSSO, respectively. Trypsin was set as the enzyme, cleaving at the C-terminal of K and R with up to 3 allowed missed cleavages. The peptide mass and length were set to be between 600-6000 Da and 6-60 amino acids, respectively. Precursor and fragment tolerances were set to 20 ppm. Carbamidomethylation [C] was set as a fixed modification, deamidation [N], and oxidation [M] were allowed as variable modifications. Results were filtered for 1% FDR, a score lower than 10e-4, and cross-links present in at least 2 out of 3 replicates.

passages.text: Structural Insights Into Complement Inhibition: Visualizing Distinct Binding Modes of C4b-Binding Protein Complexes With C4b and SAP

C4b-binding protein (C4BP) is an innate immune inhibitor found in serum. Human C4BP adopts spider-like higher-order structures (HOS) formed by disulfide-linked C4BPα and C4BPβ chains that non-covalently bind vitamin K-dependent protein S (ProS). These spider-like structures can form even larger complexes as C4BP interacts with other, mostly complement-related, proteins. The complement inhibitory role of C4BP is primarily mediated through its interaction with C4b. C4BP also binds with high affinity to serum amyloid P component (SAP), a pentraxin family member associated with amyloidosis conditions. Here, we structurally and compositionally characterize C4BP interactions with these two natively occurring binders. To achieve this, we combine mass photometry, high-speed atomic force microscopy, and cross-linking mass spectrometry. By integrating the results, we reveal two distinct binding modes of C4BP when bound to C4b or SAP. Given the spider-like assembly of C4BP, C4b interacts with the N-terminal region of a single C4BPα leg, enabling multiple C4b molecules to bind to the C4BP HOS. Conversely, SAP engages with the entire spider-like HOS: the C4BPα-C4BPβ oligomerization core binds to SAP, and the C4BPα legs wrap around it.
Graphical Abstract
Highlights
Integrative approach to study complexes of spider-like C4b-binding protein (C4BP).
When bound to C4b and SAP, C4BP reveals two distinct binding modes.
C4b binds one C4BPα, enabling multiple C4b to attach to C4BP spider-like assembly.
SAP engages the entire C4BP structure, mainly through C4BP's oligomerization core.
The distinct binding modes enable simultaneous binding of SAP and C4b to one C4BP.
In Brief

Here, we used an integrative approach to study key interactions of a spider-like complement inhibitor from human serum, C4b-binding protein (C4BP). We characterized interactions with complement C4b and serum amyloid P component (SAP) related to C4BP’s complement-inhibiting activity. Our results revealed two distinct binding mechanisms for these interactions. C4b binding involves distal domains of a single C4BPα, and SAP interaction engages the entire spider-like structure through the oligomerization core region.

The complement system serves as the first line of defense in our innate immune system. Complement activation is a series of proteolytic steps initiated by three distinct pathways: the classical, lectin, and alternative. Each of these pathways leads to the formation of C3 and C5 convertases, is accompanied by the release of anaphylatoxins, and results in the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC). The complement cascade requires precise regulation to avoid excessive inflammation that could ultimately result in sepsis. This regulation is achieved by soluble and membrane-bound complement inhibitors. Principally, these inhibitors either disrupt C3 and C5 convertases by interacting with core protein members or they can directly mediate the decay of complement proteins. Among others, human serum contains two soluble complement inhibitors: factor H (FH) and C4b-binding protein (C4BP), both of which serve as essential cofactors for the serine protease factor I (FI).

Structural models of C4b-binding protein, complement C4b, and serum amyloid P component. A, structural model of the C4BP α7β1+ProS variant formed by three chains: C4BPα (blue), C4BPβ (green), and vitamin K-dependent protein S (gray). Bottom part shows a cartoon of the C4BP HOS and C4BPα chain structure composed of eight complement control protein (CCP) domains and the C-terminal oligomerization core region. B, X-ray structure of complement C4b PDB: 5JTW, composed of C4bα (maroon), C4bβ (orange), and C4bγ (salmon). The C4d fragment (pink) is cleaved from the C4bα in the FI-mediated degradation of C4b. C, X-ray structure of SAP pentamer PDB: 1SAC in yellow with the B-face on top. All models are scaled proportionally, the scalebar corresponds to 10 nm.

Unlike the single-chain protein factor H, C4BP is formed by disulfide-linked C4BPα and C4BPβ chains. Furthermore, the C4BPβ chain interacts non-covalently with vitamin K-dependent protein S (ProS). The three chains—C4BPα, C4BPβ, and ProS—form spider-like higher-order structures (HOS) in human serum (Fig. 1A). These HOS with different co-occurring stoichiometries (α7, α7β1+ProS, and α6β1+ProS) are referred to as C4BP variants or isoforms. Regardless of their composition, all C4BP variants interact with complement factor C4b and mediate its inactivation. In this process, FI cleaves a ∼43-kDa C4d fragment from the C4b α-chain (Fig. 1B), and C4BP acts as an essential cofactor. The cleavage of C4b generates inactive C4b (iC4b), which cannot contribute to the formation of C3 and C5 convertases and consequently blocks further activation of the complement cascade.

Notwithstanding its name, C4b is not the only interacting partner of C4BP. Similar to its interaction with C4b, C4BP interacts with C3b and facilitates its FI-mediated decay. Furthermore, C4BP has been shown to bind several other biomolecules, such as heparin, DNA, or the pentraxin family members, including serum amyloid P component (SAP). Yet, the full biological context of the majority of these various C4BP interactions remains unclear.

The C4BP-SAP interaction is of particular interest, as previous reports suggested that a substantial portion of human serum C4BP is bound to SAP. Unlike monomeric C4b, SAP forms torus-shaped pentamers in human serum (Fig. 1C), a structure typical of pentraxin family members, including C-reactive protein. Under specific conditions, the SAP pentamers can form larger assemblies and aggregate while still preserving the pentameric building blocks. This SAP behavior has been implicated in amyloidosis conditions. Interestingly, the interaction with SAP has been proposed to impact C4BP's complement-inhibiting activity, further linking SAP with the complement cascade and immune response regulation.

While both SAP and C4b interactions with C4BP are crucial for C4BP's role in complement inhibition, the structural understanding of the C4BP-C4b and C4BP-SAP complexes is incomplete. The N-terminus of the C4BPα chain has been identified as essential for C4b decay, as demonstrated by mutational analysis of complement control domains (CCP) domains and specific residues. Cleaving off the C4BPα CCP1-7 with chymotrypsin suggested that SAP binds to the C4BPα C-terminal oligomerization core or CCP8. Nevertheless, these pioneering approaches were limited by their spatial resolution and could not identify binding stoichiometries. Hence, we still lack a comprehensive picture of these interactions, particularly focusing on the full-length C4BP HOS and its C4b and SAP binding sites.

Here, we aimed to characterize the aforementioned interactions of full-length C4BP HOS with C4b and SAP and their potential crosstalk. To achieve this, we combined several approaches to elucidate the binding modes of C4b and SAP to full-length C4BP and single-chain C4BPα. We examined the binding stoichiometries of C4BP complexes with C4b and SAP by single-particle mass photometry (MP). Interaction interfaces of C4BP-C4b and C4BP-SAP complexes were mapped by cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS). By integrating these results with high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), we identified unique binding mechanisms for both the C4BP-C4b and the C4BP-SAP interactions, providing detailed structural insights into these complexes.
Experimental Procedures
Experimental Design and Statistical Rationale

In this study, several techniques were combined to characterize the binding mechanisms of C4BP-C4b and C4BP-SAP complexes. Human plasma-purified protein samples (C4BP, C4b, and FI) and recombinantly expressed proteins (C4BPα and SAP) were used. The C4BP, C4b, and FI samples (Complement Technology, Inc.) were purified from healthy, pooled plasma of more than 16 donors. The recombinant SAP was analyzed by native MS, and binding stoichiometries of the recombinant SAP and human serum-derived SAP were compared by MP and did not suggest any dissimilarities (Supplemental Fig. S1). C4BPα was recombinantly expressed without the oligomerization core region (Supplemental Fig. S2). This construct was used to validate our findings on the full-length human plasma-derived proteins. XL-MS was performed in experimental triplicates, and only restraints observed in at least two out of three replicates were considered. The MP and XL-MS analyses were complemented by HS-AFM, with 66 C4BP-C4b and 33 C4BP-SAP complexes identified and characterized.
Materials and Chemicals

If not otherwise stated, all experiments were conducted using Milli-Q H2O generated by the IQ 7003 system (Merck). Trypsin and LysC were acquired from Promega and Wako, respectively. Calcium chloride, chloroacetamide (CAA), dithiothreitol (DTT), ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) disodium salt dihydrate, iodoacetamide (IAA), sodium chloride, Trizma Pre-set crystals (pH 8.5), Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), and urea were acquired from Merck. Bis(2,5-dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl) glutarate (DSG), 1-(2,5-Dioxocyclopentyl) 8-(2,5-dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl) octanedioate (DSS), and bis(2,5-Dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl) 3,3′-sulfinyldipropionate (DSSO) were acquired from CF Plus Chemicals. SDS-PAGE was performed using vendor-provided protocol with Criterion XT Bis-Tris 4 to 12% Precast gels, respective electrophoretic cells, XT Sample Buffer, XT MOPS Running Buffer, and Precision Plus Protein Dual Color Standard, all acquired from Biorad. Formic acid (FA), 4-(2-Hydroxyethyl)piperazine-1-ethane-sulfonic acid (HEPES), and trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) were acquired from Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc. LC-MS solvents A (0.1% v/v FA in H2O) and B (80% acetonitrile (ACN) v/v, 0.1% FA v/v) were acquired from Biosolve Chimie. 4-Ethylmorpholine was acquired from Fluka. C4BP, C4b, and FI were purified from pooled plasma of more than 16 healthy donors (Complement Technology, Inc). C4BPα was recombinantly expressed (Supplemental Fig. S2) in Expi293F cells with ExpiFectamine, Opti-MEM, and Expi293 expression medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the vendor-provided manual. The protein was purified using the 6xHis-tag on a Ni-NTA column. The sample was loaded in a buffer containing 50 mM NaH2PO4, 300 mM NaCl, pH 8.0, and washed with the loading buffer supplemented with 10 mM and 30 mM imidazole, respectively. The protein was eluted with 50 mM NaH2PO4, 300 mM NaCl, 0.5 M Imidazole, pH 6.3, and buffer exchanged to PBS using Ultra Centrifugal filter units (Merck). Human serum SAP was acquired from Merck, and recombinant SAP (pentraxin) was a kind gift from Dietmar Reusch and Markus Haberger.

The C4BP complexes with C4b were formed as previously described. Briefly, 0.1 mg/ml C4BP (final concentration) was incubated (37 °C, 1 h, 350 rpm) with C4b to achieve the desired molar ratio in 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl. The C4BP-SAP complexes were prepared in a similar manner to the C4BP complexes with C4b. C4BP 0.1 mg/ml (final concentration) was incubated with SAP to achieve the desired molar ratio (37 °C, 1 h, 350 rpm) in 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2.
Data presented here were partially post-processed using the following Python libraries: matplotlib, NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, and seaborn.
Mass Photometry

MP experiments were conducted either on the OneMP or the SamuxMP (both Refeyn Ltd), depending on the expected molecular weight (MW) of the analyzed species. Specifically, C4BP-C4b complexes with expected MW above ∼1 MDa were analyzed on the SamuxMP for its better sensitivity in this higher MW region. Samples containing C4BPα were analyzed preferentially on the OneMP, as the SamuxMP does not accurately detect species with an MW lower than ∼150 kDa. The C4BP-SAP samples were analyzed on both instruments.

The samples were analyzed on in-house carrier slides that were prepared from microscope coverslips (24 mm × 50 mm; Paul Marienfeld GmbH) and reusable cell culture gaskets (Grace Biolabs). Prior to the measurement, 12 μl of buffer was used for the automatic focusing procedure. Subsequently, 3 μl of the sample was added, resulting in the final sample concentration of ∼10 nM. Data were recorded for 60 to 120 s at a scan rate of 100 frames per second. Measurements for the C4b complexes were carried out in 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, while the SAP complexes were analyzed in 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2. The C4PB-SAP samples treated with 10 mM EDTA were diluted in 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, 10 mM EDTA to achieve the final sample concentration ∼50 nM and incubated 10 min at room temperature (RT) prior to the measurement.

The raw MP movies were analyzed and mass-calibrated in DiscoverMP (Refeyn Ltd). For the OneMP, the calibration was performed with IgG-halfbody (73 kDa), IgG (149 kDa), apoferritin (513 kDa), and IgM (1006 kDa). The SamuxMP calibration was performed using bovine thyroglobulin in different oligomeric states (335 kDa, 670 kDa, 1005 kDa, and 1340 kDa). The calibrated events were exported and analyzed as previously described. The resulting mass distributions were plotted as histograms with a bin size of 10 kDa for the SamuxMP and 5 kDa for the OneMP and manually annotated.
Cross-Linking Mass Spectrometry

Cross-linking was performed in an experimental triplicate with DSS, DSG, and DSSO, all at 0.5 mM concentration, based on prior optimization (Supplemental Fig. S3). All complexes were prepared as described above (37 °C, 1 h, 350 rpm) in 2:1 C4BPα:C4b, 2:1 SAP:C4BP, 1:1 C4BP:C4b molar ratios. The reaction was performed for 1 h, RT in 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, and 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2 for the C4b and the SAP complexes, respectively. The addition of a crosslinker resulted in a final DMSO concentration of 5% (v/v) in the sample. Immediately after the 1 h incubation, the reaction was quenched with 1 M Tris (pH 8.5) to achieve a final concentration of 50 mM in the sample. The cross-linked samples were denatured by 8 M urea. Reduction and alkylation were performed with 10 mM TCEP and 40 mM CAA (30 min, RT). After the samples were diluted with N-ethylmorpholine buffer (pH 8.5), to reduce the urea concentration to 2 M. The samples were digested by trypsin (1:20 (w/w)) and LysC (1:50 (w/w)) for 16h, 37 °C. The digestion was stopped by TFA addition (final 0.5% (v/v)), and the resulting peptides were desalted on an Oasis HLB μElution Plate (Waters Corp) using a vendor-provided protocol. Solvent from the desalted peptides was fully evaporated, and the peptides were deglycosylated using a Protein Deglycosylation Mix II (New England Biolabs) according to the non-denaturing vendor-provided protocol. The deglycosylated peptides were desalted, and the solvent was fully evaporated. Before the MS analysis, the peptides were dissolved in 2% (v/v) FA.

The liquid chromatography (LC)-MS/MS analysis was performed on an UltiMate 3000 UHPLC system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc). The cross-linked peptides were analyzed in a 90 min gradient. First, the peptides were trapped on an Acclaim Pepmap 100 C18 (5 mm × 0.3 mm, 5 μm, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc) for 1 min at a flow rate of 30 μl/min, solvent A (0.1% FA v/v in H2O). The trapping was followed by a separation on an analytical column packed in-house (Reprosil 2.4 μm, 75 μm × 50 cm) at a flow rate of 0.3 μl/min using a gradient starting from 9% solvent B (80% acetonitrile (ACN) v/v, 0.1% FA v/v) at 0 to 1 min, 13% B at 2 min, 44% B at 67 min, 55% B 72 min, 99% B 75 min, and equilibrated for the next run in 9% B at 80 to 90 min. MS1 scans were collected with the following parameters: resolution = 60,000, mass range = 375 to 1600 Th, automatic AGC target and maximum injection time, cycle time = 1 s. MS2 scans were collected in data-dependent mode for precursors with charge state above 3, with the following parameters: isolation window = 1.4 Th, resolution = 30,000, mass range = 200 to 2000 Th. Precursors that were once selected for fragmentation were excluded from MS2 for 30 s. The peptides were fragmented using stHCD with NCE 19, 25, 31% for DSSO, and NCE 24, 28, 33% for DSG and DSS.

The resulting raw spectra were searched using pLink 2 against a FASTA file containing common contaminants (pLink 2, 293 entries) and the most abundant proteins with IBAQ > 9.5 × 106 from the C4BP sample (25 entries; UniProt accessed: 10/10/2023), as identified by bottom-up proteomics. Additionally, the C4A and C4B genes were divided into three separate chains (α, β, and γ), which form the C4b structure. Propeptides and signal peptides of C4BPα, C4BPβ, ProS, and C4b were removed from the FASTA file, and SAP sequence was added. In the case of the C4b complex with recombinant C4BPα, the C4BPα sequence was substituted by the recombinant protein sequence (Supplemental Fig. S2). The linker mass cross-linking two lysine residues was set to be 96.021 Da, 138.068 Da, and 158.004 Da for DSG, DSS, and DSSO, respectively. Trypsin was set as the enzyme, cleaving at the C-terminal of K and R with up to 3 allowed missed cleavages. The peptide mass and length were set to be between 600 to 6000 Da and 6 to 60 amino acids, respectively. Precursor and fragment tolerances were set to 20 ppm. Carbamidomethylation [C] was set as a fixed modification, deamidation [N], and oxidation [M] were allowed as variable modifications. Results were filtered for 1% FDR, a score lower than 10e-4, and cross-links present in at least two out of three replicates (Supplemental Tables S1–S3). The filtered results were visualized in xiVIEW. Unless otherwise stated, all residue numbers refer to the full-length proteins, including propeptides and signal peptides, based on respective UniProt entries. Structural visualizations were performed in ChimeraX using the XMAS bundle. The pLink2 search results were compared to xiSEARCH, as described in Supplemental Figure S4.
High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy

The C4BP-C4b and C4BP-SAP samples for HS-AFM were prepared as described above in 1:3 and 1:1 M ratios, respectively. HS-AFM (RIBM) was conducted in tapping mode at RT in buffer, with free amplitudes of 1.5 to 2.5 nm and amplitude set points larger than 90%. Silicon nitride cantilevers with electron-beam deposited tips (USC-F1.2-k0.15, Nanoworld AG), nominal spring constants of 0.15 N/m, resonance frequencies around 500 kHz, and a quality factor of ∼2 in liquids were used.

C4BP-C4b complexes or unbound C4b were diluted to 1 to 4 μg/ml C4BP using weak immobilization buffer (75 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris, 5 mM MgCl2, pH 7.4) and incubated on freshly cleaved muscovite mica for 1 to 6 min, followed by three washing steps using strong immobilization buffer (75 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris, 10 mM NiCl2, pH 7.4). Imaging was performed in a strong immobilization buffer.

C4BP-SAP complexes, as well as unbound C4BP and unbound SAP, were diluted to 1 to 4 μg/ml C4BP using SAP buffer (50 mM HEPES, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM CaCl2, pH 7.4) and incubated on freshly cleaved muscovite mica for 1 to 6 min, followed by three washing steps using strong immobilization buffer. Imaging was performed in the strong immobilization buffer. Images were processed using Gwyddion 2.62 and ImageJ (NIH). The ImageJ plugin “Linear Stack Alignment with SIFT” was used for drift correction where indicated.
C4BP-Mediated C4b Inactivation

C4BP activity in mediating C4b degradation was assessed as described previously. Briefly, C4BP or C4BPα 50 μg/ml, C4b 100 μg/ml, and FI 5 μg/ml were mixed in 50 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, and incubated (37 °C, 15 min, 350 rpm). The final mixture was incubated (37 °C, 15 min, 350 rpm). Immediately after the incubation, the samples were denatured by adding XT Sample Buffer with 25 mM DTT and heated (95 °C, 5 min). The resulting samples were analyzed by SDS-PAGE using a vendor-provided protocol. SDS-PAGE gels were stained in Imperial Protein Stain (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc). To evaluate C4b degradation, the incubation time and concentrations were optimized to detect undigested C4b α-chain and the C4d fragment generated from C4b α-chain by C4BP-mediated digestion by FI.
Results

To investigate the C4BP HOS and its role in complement inhibition, we aimed to characterize two key interactions of C4BP with previously proposed, natively occurring, binding partners: C4b and SAP. In healthy donor serum, C4BP ∼30 mg/L, SAP ∼25 mg/L, and C4 ∼300 mg/L are substantially abundant. Notably, the protein concentrations vary under certain conditions. The activated C4b concentrations are lower than C4 and depend on the extent of complement activation. C4BP concentration also increases during acute-phase inflammation. Still, given the protein concentrations in healthy serum and the reported high affinities between C4BP-C4b KD ∼8 nM and C4BP-SAP KD ∼22 nM, all these interactions could co-occur in human serum. Therefore, they are crucial for understanding the structure and the function of the C4BP HOS in human serum.

First, to examine binding stoichiometries of the C4BP-C4b complexes, we employed mass photometry (MP) (Fig. 2, A and B; Supplemental Fig. S5). MP is a single-particle detection technique that enables MW determination of proteins and protein complexes under native conditions. Measurements of native human C4BP purified from healthy donor serum revealed two major high-MW distributions of α6β1+ProS/α7β1 (537 ± 21 kDa) and α7β1+ProS (614 ± 28 kDa) on the OneMP (Supplemental Fig. S5), in agreement with our previous observations. With a lower resolution on the SamuxMP, native C4BP measurements result in a single, broader MW distribution composed of both C4BP variants with a mass of 574 ± 70 kDa (Fig. 2A, Supplemental Fig. S5). Measurements of the native C4b sample revealed a single mass distribution of ∼180 kDa (Supplemental Fig. S5) on both instruments.

As we were able to detect the unbound components, we proceeded with measurements of C4BP:C4b samples incubated in various molar ratios (Fig. 2A), ranging from 2:1 to 1:5. The determined MW distributions confirmed complex formation. The stoichiometries of observed complexes ranged from 1:1 (C4BP:C4b) up to 1:3 over C4b. This observation confirmed that multiple C4b molecules can bind to a single C4BP. Still, it did not fully exclude the possibility of multiple C4BPα chains from a single C4BP HOS binding to one C4b.

To explore this possibility, we analyzed mixtures of a single C4BPα with C4b (Fig. 2B). The C4BPα construct comprises all 8 CCP domains but lacks the C-terminal oligomerization region (Supplemental Fig. S2). MP analysis of the C4BPα construct revealed a single distribution corresponding to 66 ± 10 kDa. Measurements of the C4PBα:C4b samples in various ratios resulted in the formation of 1:1 C4PBα:C4b complexes (Fig. 2B). We observed an increasing fractional abundance of the complex with an increasing abundance of C4BPα. However, we did not detect any other complexes, indicating that 1:1 C4BPα:C4b is the preferred stoichiometry.

To gain a structural overview of the C4BP-C4b interaction and validate our MP observations, we used high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM). In this single-particle technique, biomolecules and their assemblies are directly imaged on a mica surface. HS-AFM imaging of unbound C4BP revealed spider-like assemblies (Fig. 3A), as described before. C4b analysis resulted in a uniform population of smaller, oval-shaped particles (Fig. 3B), corresponding to the C4b structure (Fig. 1B). The analysis of the C4BP-C4b sample revealed 66 distinct C4BP HOS particles bound to 84 C4b molecules (Fig. 3, C and D). These complexes were divided into three classes: 1:1 C4BP:C4b, 1:2 C4BP:C4b, and 1:3 C4BP:C4b complexes. The 1:1 complex was the most abundant, accounting for 76% of observed species. The remaining particles corresponded to 1:2 (21%) and 1:3 (3%) C4BP:C4b complexes. Despite the compositional difference, the C4BP-C4b interaction appeared identical in all cases. We observed N-terminal CCP domains of a single C4BPα chain bound to one C4b (Supplemental Movie S1). No evidence for multiple C4BPα chains interacting with a single C4b has been observed, suggesting that each C4BPα chain independently interacts with C4b. Furthermore, the HS-AFM analysis did not reveal evidence of the direct involvement of other C4BP HOS components, i.e., C4BPβ and ProS, in the interaction with C4b.

The HS-AFM and MP results suggested that the C4BP-C4b interaction is mediated by the distal CCP domains of the C4BPα chain. To directly identify which regions of C4BP are involved in the interaction and to localize their binding on C4b, we used cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS). This technique uses bispecific reagents to couple adjacent residues in native protein complexes to map their interaction interfaces. We generated two datasets, one for the C4BP-C4b complex and another for the C4BPα-C4b complex. The XL-MS results provided by two independent search algorithms, pLink2 and xiSEARCH, for the C4BP-C4b suggested that CCP1-4 of C4BPα interacts with C4b (Fig. 4A, Supplemental Fig. S4). The involvement of CCP1-4 is also evident from the C4BPα-C4b XL-MS restraints (Fig. 4B). This observation is consistent with HS-AFM and MP and further confirmed that neither C4BPβ nor ProS are involved in the interaction.

Examining the localization of cross-links detected in both XL-MS datasets on the C4b protein structure, we predominantly observed CCP1 and CCP4 domains of C4BPα cross-linked to distinct parts of C4b (Fig. 4, A–C, Supplemental Fig. S6). C4BPα CCP1 cross-links were uniquely detected in the CUB (complement C1r/C1s, Uegf, Bmp1) domain of C4b α-chain (Fig. 4C). Specifically, the CCP1 cross-linked residues of C4b—K1340, K1369, K1375, and K1379—all belong to the CUB domain and are localized close to the C-terminal FI cleavage site (R1336). Conversely, the C4BPα CCP4 cross-linked sites were localized in the TED (thiol ester-containing domain) and MG1 (macroglobulin domain 1). The TED is a part of the C4b α-chain, which forms a substantial part of the C4d fragment, and the cross-linked residues (K1099, K1051) are localized proximal to the N-terminal FI cleavage site (T957). We also detected CCP4 cross-links localized to MG1, a neighboring domain of TED, from the C4b β-chain. These results indicate that C4BPα CCP4 binds between C4b TED and MG1 domains, similarly to the FH CCP4-C3b interaction.

Interestingly, mapping the C4b intra-links on the experimental structure revealed several over-length cross-links (Supplemental Fig. S7). These cross-links primarily connect the CUB domain of C4b with the C345C (C3, C4, C5 complement) and TED domains. This observation indicates that the CUB domain, where FI-mediated cleavage takes place, not only interacts with C4BPα but also undergoes significant structural rearrangements upon binding. These structural changes in C4b, induced by its interaction with C4BPα, likely play a key role in the mechanism of C4BP action. This is further supported by the fact that C4BP is essential for FI-mediated degradation of C4b, and FI does not directly interact with C4BP (Supplemental Fig. S8).

Taken together, we demonstrated that a single C4BPα CCP1-4 binds to C4b, and accordingly, C4BP HOS binds multiple C4b molecules. The C4BPα-C4b interaction leads to structural rearrangements in the CUB domain of C4b, enabling the FI cleavage. The key role of a single C4BPα chain is demonstrated by the similar activity of full-length C4BP and the C4BPα construct in FI-mediated C4b degradation (Supplemental Fig. S8).

Analogous to the C4BP-C4b interaction, we next explored the C4BP-SAP interaction, first determining the preferred binding stoichiometries using MP (Fig. 5A). SAP forms torus-shaped pentamers, which were readily detected by native MS (Supplemental Fig. S1) and MP as a single MW distribution of 129 ± 11 kDa (Supplemental Fig. S9). The MP results for C4BP-SAP complexes in a buffer containing Ca2+ (Fig. 5A, bottom) revealed two major high MW populations, corresponding to both C4BP variants, α6β1+ProS/α7β1 and α7β1+ProS, forming 1:1 C4BP:SAP (pentamer) complexes. In contrast to the C4BP-C4b interaction, which exhibited a range of stoichiometries (Fig. 2A), the C4BP-SAP complexes showed a strong preference for 1:1 C4BP:SAP (pentamer) ratios, even in an excess of SAP (Fig. 5A, bottom). Furthermore, the results indicated that both C4BP variants α6β1+ProS/α7β1 and α7β1+ProS present in the pooled healthy plasma-derived C4BP sample are capable of SAP binding. We also highlighted that the C4BP-SAP complexes are formed in a Ca2+-dependent manner and are disrupted by 10 mM EDTA (Fig. 5A, top). Human serum-derived SAP exhibited the same binding behavior, further confirming these findings (Supplemental Fig. S1).

To further examine the C4BP-SAP interaction, we investigated SAP binding to the single C4BPα construct (Fig. 5B). We acquired MP data for C4BPα:SAP in 1:1 and 1:10 molar ratios. However, even with an excess of the recombinant C4BPα, we did not observe complex formation. Both measurements revealed two distinct MW distributions corresponding to unbound C4BPα and SAP. This observation suggested that the full C4BP HOS is essential for the interaction with SAP. Moreover, it hinted towards the involvement of the C4BPα-C4BPβ oligomerization core in the interaction with SAP, which is not present in the recombinant C4BPα construct.

Observing the 1:1 C4BP:SAP complexes in MP, we next aimed to directly visualize the C4BP-SAP binding and compare the overall structures of C4BP-C4b (Fig. 3) and the C4BP-SAP complexes by HS-AFM (Fig. 6). While the analysis of unbound C4BP resulted in a spider-like structure (Fig. 6A), imaging of SAP revealed a flat, round structure with a hollow center and clearly defined subunits (Fig. 6B), consistent with the previously published structure of SAP pentamer. From the 151 queried C4BP HOS, 33 particles were assigned as the C4BP-SAP complexes (Fig. 6, C and D, Supplemental Movie S2 and S3). These resembled C4BP HOS but with a thicker core region tightly surrounded by C4BPα chains. The height of these structures (∼10.5 nm) was greater than that of C4BP and SAP individually (each ∼5.5 nm) and closely matched their combined heights.

Further examination of the HS-AFM dataset allowed us to discern two classes of C4BP-SAP complexes. In class I (N = 26) (Fig. 6C, Supplemental Movie S2), the core height remained unchanged throughout the observation window, even under increased scanning forces. This suggests that the disulfide-linked C4BP oligomerization core is positioned on top of the complex, protecting the non-covalently attached SAP from dissociation. In contrast, in class II (N = 7), even minimal scanning forces induced a rapid reduction in core height (Fig. 6D, Supplemental Movie S3). We attribute this reduction to SAP pentamer dissociation from the C4BP core when SAP is positioned on top of the complex and C4BP is in direct contact with mica. We propose that the entire SAP pentamer detaches from C4BP rather than that SAP monomers sequentially dissociate, as SAP pentamer disruption occurs only at increased scanning forces (Supplemental Movie S2). For both classes of C4BP-SAP complexes, it was not possible to distinguish and annotate all C4BPα chains, suggesting their compact arrangement around the C4BP oligomerization core and their potential involvement in the interaction with SAP. For class II complexes, direct electrostatic interaction with the mica substrate reduced C4BPα mobility and forced the entire C4BP HOS to adopt a flat conformation. This likely affected C4BP's interaction with SAP, as indicated by the lower abundance and shorter lifetime of these complexes.

The MP and HS-AFM results pointed to the C4BP oligomerization core involvement in C4BP-SAP complex formation. Yet, to directly confirm this hypothesis and to map the interaction interfaces of C4BP-SAP, we used XL-MS. In the case of C4BP-SAP, we acquired experimental data only for the full-length C4BP HOS complexes (Fig. 7A, Supplemental Fig. S10), as the single C4BPα construct did not interact with SAP (Fig. 5B). The XL-MS results from two independent search algorithms, pLink2 and xiSEARCH, confirmed that C4BP binds to SAP through the oligomerization core (Fig. 7, Supplemental Fig. S4). We identified cross-links of the C-terminal alpha-helical region of C4BPα and C4BPβ with SAP, as well as cross-links in the CCP8 domain of C4BPα chain. Interestingly, we also observed several cross-links of the N-terminal CCP1 of C4BPα with SAP. This distal domain is also involved in the interaction with C4b (Fig. 4, A and B). Examining the C4BPα CCP1, we also observed a self-link (orange) of the CCP1. This self-link was not observed in the C4BP-C4b XL-MS experiment and is likely reflective of C4BPα chains being closer together while interacting with SAP, as visualized by HS-AFM (Fig. 6, C and D, Supplemental Movie S2 and S3).

The SAP pentamer, like other pentraxin family members, consists of two faces (Fig. 7B): the A-face with the ridge helix and the B-face which binds Ca2+ ions. In the XL-MS experiments, we detected five lysine residues: 26, 84, 98, 149, 162, and α-amino group of His 20 (N-terminus, after the signal peptide cleavage) from the SAP structure cross-linked to C4BPα (Fig. 7, A and C). Additionally, we detected several cross-links between C4BPβ K213 and SAP K162. To map the C4BP interaction interface on SAP pentamer, we classified the C4BPα-SAP cross-links based on the C4BP domains for each of the SAP cross-linked sites (Fig. 7C). For C4BPα CCP8 and the C4BPα oligomerization core alpha-helix, we observed 31 cross-link spectrum matches (CSMs) each. For C4BPα CCP1, we detected 18 CSMs. Interestingly, SAP sites K84 and K98, localized on the B-face, were uniquely cross-linked to the oligomerization core region. In contrast, K26 (localized on the A-face) and K20 (N-terminus localized on the outer side of the pentamer facing the A-face) were preferentially cross-linked to the CCP1 region. SAP K162, located on the outer side of the pentamer facing the B-face, was cross-linked to all parts of C4BPα, although there was a stronger preference for cross-linking with CCP8.

These XL-MS results align well with the HS-AFM data (Fig. 6, C and D, Supplemental Movie S2 and S3). In the HS-AFM, we observed C4BP-SAP complexes interacting through the oligomerization core. Based on the XL-MS results, we conclude that SAP interacts with the C4BP oligomerization core preferentially via its B-face. This binding mode is evidenced by the unique cross-links of C4BPα oligomerization core K595 to SAP K84 and K98 (Fig. 7C, Supplemental Fig. S11). This finding agrees with our MP results, showing no interaction between C4BPα lacking the oligomerization core region and SAP. The B-face-mediated binding is further supported by the Ca2+-dependent nature of the interaction (Fig. 4A). Considering the sizes of the C4BP oligomerization core and the SAP pentamer (Figs. 1, 6, A and B), it is likely that the inner part of the SAP pentamer interacts with the C4BP oligomerization core, while the CCP8 and the CCP1 domains of C4BP can engage with the sides and residues localized on the A-face of the pentamer. This A-face interaction is evidenced by the unique cross-links between CCP1 and CCP8 with SAP K26.

In summary, our results highlighted that the C4BP HOS variants form 1:1 complexes with SAP pentamer. This interaction is mediated by the B-face of SAP binding to the C4BP oligomerization core region, while the C4BPα CCP domains can wrap around and engage with the A-face of SAP.
Discussion

Here, we explored the role of the spider-like complement inhibitor from human serum C4BP by characterizing its interactions with two natively occurring binding partners: C4b and SAP. Our results structurally and compositionally describe these interactions, uncovering two distinct binding modes for C4b and SAP. Our data revealed that C4b interacts with the distal CCP domains 1 to 4 of a single C4BPα chain, which leads to multiple C4b molecules bound to a single C4BP HOS. In contrast, SAP pentamer binding engages the full C4BP HOS, and the interaction is primarily mediated by C4BP's oligomerization core region and proximal CCP8 binding to the B-side of SAP.

Taking a closer look at the interaction interfaces of the C4BP-C4b complex, we detected that CCP1-4 from a single C4BPα interact close to the FI cleavage sites on the C4b α-chain. The critical role of the distal C4BPα CCP domains aligns with previous reports showing that deletion or replacement of C4BPα CCP1-3, or an extended link between CCP3-4, significantly reduces C4BP's activity in mediating C4b degradation. Additional mutational studies confined the interaction interface responsible for C4b binding and degradation to a cluster of positively charged residues within CCP1-3 of C4BPα. Interestingly, one of these C4BPα mutants, K126Q/K128Q (corresponding to K174 and K176 in the UniProt annotation), lost its activity but still interacted with C4b. Our data might support this observation, as we detected cross-links involving both K174 and K176. Specifically, these residues were linked to K1646 in the C345 domain of the C4b γ-chain and K1340 in the CUB domain of the C4b α-chain (Supplemental Table S1 and S2, Fig. S6), suggesting their role in the structural rearrangement of the CUB domain, which is likely essential for FI cleavage. Nonetheless, the C4BP-C4b interaction is heavily reliant on CCP1 and CCP4 (Figs. 4, Supplemental Figs S6 and S7), which clarifies why these mutations in CCP3 do not disrupt the interaction.

In contrast to the C4BP-C4b interaction, SAP binding to C4BP requires the full HOS. Our data revealed that this Ca2+-mediated interaction with the B-face of SAP is predominantly dependent on the C-terminal oligomerization core and CCP8 of C4BPα. This finding is consistent with previously proposed coarse binding interfaces based on biophysical analyses with proteolytically truncated C4BP. Notably, beyond refining these interaction interfaces, we also identified a novel interaction involving CCP1 and the A-face of SAP. This suggests that the C4BP HOS engages both faces of the SAP pentamer and effectively wraps around it.

Interestingly, a previous report proposed crosstalk between C4BP interactions with SAP and C4b, i.e., that SAP binding reduces the complement-inhibiting activity of C4BP. Our data provide a possible structural explanation for this observation. It has been proposed that C4BPα CCP1 is crucial for the interaction with C4b, which is followed by FI-mediated degradation of C4b. Our XL-MS experiment indicated that CCP1 interacts with the CUB domain of C4b, located near the FI cleavage site (Fig. 4). This structurally explains the role of C4BPα CCP1 and highlights its importance in C4b degradation. Remarkably, we observed cross-links between C4BPα CCP1 and SAP (Fig. 7), revealing the dual role of CCP1 in interacting with both C4b and SAP. This, together with the reduced flexibility of C4BPα chains observed in HS-AFM upon SAP binding, can explain the reduced complement-inhibiting activity of the C4BP-SAP complex compared to unbound C4BP. While both C4b and SAP can simultaneously bind to C4BP HOS (Supplemental Fig. S9), it is evident that SAP binding reduces the flexibility of C4BPα chains (Supplemental Movie S1–S3). The reduced flexibility of C4BPα chains, combined with SAP sterically hindering the attachment of multiple C4b molecules to the C4BP-SAP complex, likely leads to the reduced complement-inhibiting activity of SAP-bound C4BP.

The C4b, SAP, and C4BP crosstalk suggests that the strong C4BP-SAP interaction could act as an additional regulatory mechanism within the complement cascade. Although SAP binding has previously been proposed only on surfaces, our results clearly demonstrated that C4BP-SAP binding can occur in solution. Relevance of the C4BP-SAP interaction in serum is further supported by its low KD ∼22 nM, which is below normal serum concentration of both ∼50 nM C4BP and ∼200 nM SAP. Thus, we propose that SAP binding may affect the complement-inhibiting function of C4BP HOS in circulation, especially as protein concentrations fluctuate during the acute-phase response. Particularly, C4BP, or more precisely C4BPα, concentrations increase dramatically during acute-phase inflammation. Consequently, both the levels of C4BP increase and the proportion of more active, SAP-unbound C4BP also rises. This further links SAP to complement cascade regulation and is structurally underlined by the involvement of CCP1 in interactions with both C4b and SAP.

In conclusion, we provide novel structural insights into the interactions of full-length C4BP HOS with C4b and SAP by employing an integrative structural proteomics approach combining MP, HS-AFM, and XL-MS. This approach enabled us to determine the binding stoichiometries of the C4BP-C4b and C4BP-SAP complexes, directly visualize their structures, and map the interaction interfaces of all binding partners. Our findings reveal two distinct binding modes. The C4BP-C4b interaction is mediated by the N-terminal CCP1-4 of a single C4BPα chain, while the C4BP-SAP interaction is mediated by the C-terminal oligomerization core and involves the entire spider-like structure. Importantly, these novel structural insights provide a structural basis for the C4BP-C4b-SAP crosstalk and further connect SAP with complement cascade regulation.
